description: We’re Malay Sourav and Ramneek Kaur, two students based in Paderborn, Germany, who like turning messy data into tools people can actually use. For Space Apps 2026 we built Freefall Fire Atlas, a dashboard that turns NASA’s microgravity combustion experiments into fire-safety insights for future Moon and Mars habitats.
summary:
Fire in space doesn’t behave like fire on Earth. Without gravity, hot air doesn’t rise, so a flame only gets oxygen from the cabin’s airflow. What caught our attention: NASA’s Moon base may run at around 30% oxygen, and the fires on Apollo 1, Apollo 13 and Mir all involved extra oxygen.

So we built Freefall Fire Atlas. It turns NASA’s 24 microgravity combustion investigations (about 2,000 test runs) into a Fire Scenario Explorer. Pick a habitat and a type of fire, and it ranks the studies that matter for each stage: smoke, ignition, spread and suppression. It explains every score, shows how close NASA’s tests came to your habitat’s oxygen and pressure, and flags where no data exists yet, like partial gravity.

AI summarizes each investigation and answers questions only from NASA’s records, always citing DOIs. It’s a research and learning tool, not something to make real safety decisions with.
details:
What it does and how it works

Our project, Freefall Fire Atlas, is a web dashboard that helps you make sense of NASA's microgravity combustion research. Fire behaves really differently in space — without gravity there's no buoyancy, so a flame can't pull in fresh air on its own and instead depends on the cabin's airflow. NASA has run 24 combustion investigations in orbit (in the ISS glovebox and combustion rack, and on Cygnus cargo vehicles after they leave the station) — about 2,000 individual test runs in total. The problem is that all of it lives in NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics archive spread across 19 differently-shaped tables that are genuinely hard to compare. So we pulled it together, standardized 1,858 of those runs into one clean table, and built a tool on top.

The way it works: you pick a habitat (the ISS, a Moon base, a planned exploration habitat, or a spacesuit) and a fire scenario, like an electrical overheat. The app then ranks which NASA investigations actually matter for each phase of that fire — smoke, ignition, spread, and suppression — and, importantly, it explains why each one ranks where it does instead of just handing you a black-box score. A "gap map" plots every test by oxygen and pressure so you can literally see how far the real experiments are from the atmosphere you care about, and warning cards flag things like the ISS smoke detector's known blind spot for the tiny particles that come off overheated Kapton and Teflon wiring.

Benefits and intended impact

The honest value is time and clarity. A student or researcher can see in a couple of minutes which experiments apply to, say, a 30%-oxygen Moon base, how close the data really is, and — the part we care about most — what still hasn't been tested. For instance, there's no partial-gravity combustion data at all yet (the Moon and Mars sit somewhere between microgravity and Earth), so we flag that gap and point to the upcoming FM2 and LUCI experiments. We also surface that Earth flammability tests aren't always conservative: PMMA plastic kept spreading at 17% oxygen in microgravity but not at 18% on Earth. We deliberately built this as a research and reference tool, not an operational safety system — it never calls a material "safe," only reports what the tests show or where there's no data.

Tools we used

It's all Python so we could realistically build and ship it in a weekend: pandas for the data pipeline, Streamlit for the app, Plotly for the charts, sentence-transformers with FAISS for an "Ask" feature that answers questions only from NASA's own text (and cites the DOIs), and Google Gemini for the optional written answers. We wrote the ranking and warning logic as plain, transparent code, and used pytest to keep ourselves honest. It's hosted on Streamlit Community Cloud.

What makes it creative, and what we weighed

A lot of tools stop at just mapping the data. Our twist is the phase-by-phase scenario ranking with plain-English explanations, and the oxygen-partial-pressure framing — the slightly counterintuitive point that the exploration habitat actually has lower oxygen partial pressure than the ISS but a higher oxygen fraction, which makes materials ignite and spread more easily. The thing we argued about most was data honesty: we never fill blank cells with zeros, and we never assume a pressure value that NASA didn't record — even though that means some famous experiments drop off the gap map. We'd rather show an honest gap than a confident-looking wrong number. And because PSI requires it, every claim in the app links back to its DOI.

The full source code is public on GitHub: https://github.com/malay24/freefall-fire-atlas
